name: Policosanol
lead: Policosanol is a mixture of long-chain primary alcohols, chiefly octacosanol, extracted from plant waxes such as sugarcane wax and sold as a dietary supplement for blood cholesterol.[1][2] It was first developed commercially in Cuba, where Dalmer Laboratories produced the first supplements.[1][2]

In the wiki's appearance framework it belongs to the metabolic-health group: people take it for lipid, blood-sugar and liver-enzyme markers, which are part of the general health profile behind body composition, energy and training capacity. Meta-analyses of randomised trials have reported small reductions in blood glucose and in liver enzymes.[9][10] No trial has measured body fat or visible appearance as an outcome.

The cholesterol research is contested. Early Cuban trials reported lower cholesterol, but a randomized trial published in JAMA in 2006 and a 2008 trial found no lipid lowering, and Wikipedia notes that groups outside Cuba have not reproduced the Cuban results.[3][4][11][2] A 2018 meta-analysis of 22 studies cited by Wikipedia reported improved lipid profiles, and the European Food Safety Authority rejected a cholesterol health claim in 2011, according to Grokipedia.[2][1]
infobox: Dietary supplement; EFSA rejected a cholesterol claim in 2011 [1]

paras: Policosanol is a mixture of alcohols with roughly 24 to 34 carbons; in sugarcane extracts octacosanol makes up the majority, with triacontanol and hexacosanol as lesser components [1][2]. The same alcohols occur in beeswax and cereal waxes [1][2].

Laboratory studies reported that policosanol inhibits cholesterol synthesis in hepatoma cells via AMP-kinase activation [5] and modulates HMG-CoA reductase activity in cultured fibroblasts [6]. These are cell studies.

The first policosanol supplements were produced by Dalmer Laboratories in Cuba, and studies from the Cuban group reported it as safe and effective for lowering lipids, although those studies were small and mostly came from one institute.[2] The JAMA 2006 trial describes more than 80 placebo-controlled or comparative trials, performed mostly by a single research institute, suggesting lipid-lowering effects comparable with statins.[4]

Wikipedia says groups outside Cuba have not replicated those results and that, as of 2010, policosanol was marketed as a lipid-lowering agent in the Caribbean, Central and South America and Canada.[2] It can also be isolated from beeswax, cereal grains, grasses, leaves, fruits, nuts and seeds.[2]
A 2002 review of placebo-controlled studies concluded policosanol lowered cholesterol in volunteers and patients with type II hypercholesterolemia.[3]

The 2006 JAMA trial was a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 143 patients with hypercholesterolemia or combined hyperlipidemia, with a 12-week double-blind phase. In no group did LDL cholesterol fall more than 10 percent from baseline or differ significantly from placebo, there were no significant effects on total cholesterol, HDL, triglycerides or lipoprotein(a), and the treatment was well tolerated with no serious adverse events.[4] A 2008 double-blind trial of Cuban sugarcane policosanol in 68 people with primary hypercholesterolemia likewise reported no lipid changes.[11]

A 12-week randomised trial in healthy Japanese adults reported lower blood pressure, HbA1c and liver enzymes and about 9.5 percent higher HDL cholesterol than placebo.[12] Meta-analyses of randomised trials found small reductions in blood glucose (25 trials, 2,680 participants, about 2 mg/dl) and in ALT and AST (23 trials, 2,535 participants).[9][10] A 2018 meta-analysis of 22 studies reported improved dyslipidemia, per Wikipedia.[2]

A 2017 Italian position statement and a 2016 meta-analysis of nutraceutical combinations discuss its role among supplements.[7][8] A registered 120-person trial of policosanol and exercise on fitness and lipids is listed as not yet recruiting.[13] No studies of policosanol for fat loss or body composition have been published.

EFSA rejected health claims for maintaining normal cholesterol in 2011, according to Grokipedia [1]. Wikipedia describes it as marketed as a lipid-lowering agent in parts of the Caribbean, Latin America and Canada, and says human consumption was described as safe and well tolerated in a 2005 meta-analysis [2].
A pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic study examined policosanol alongside warfarin in healthy subjects.[14]
Policosanol is sold as capsules or tablets, often in combination cholesterol-support products, and the studies describe daily oral use for weeks to months.[4][12]

card.summary: A sugarcane-wax alcohol mixture sold for cholesterol, with disputed lipid results and no evidence on body fat or looks.
card.note: Cuban trials were positive but non-Cuban replications were not; not studied for appearance.

quick.overview:
Policosanol is a mix of waxy alcohols from sugarcane, sold as a cholesterol supplement. It comes from Cuban research in the 1990s.

Cuban studies reported lower cholesterol, but later trials elsewhere did not replicate this, and it has not been studied for fat loss or appearance.
quick.mechanism: Cell studies suggest it may suppress cholesterol synthesis via AMP-kinase and effects on HMG-CoA reductase; human effects are disputed.
quick.risks: A 2005 meta-analysis described it as well tolerated, per Wikipedia. EFSA rejected a cholesterol claim in 2011, per Grokipedia.

chain: Supplement taken daily for blood-lipid and metabolic markers
Markers such as glucose, liver enzymes and HDL may shift modestly in some trials
Supports the metabolic health that underpins leanness and training capacity
angle.text: People use policosanol as part of a metabolic-health stack for cholesterol, blood sugar and liver markers, which are relevant to staying lean and training. It is not marketed or tested as a direct appearance product.
